English Wikipedia and Wikidata (Q65077764, no P625) place the town only on the Corycus/Gramvousa peninsula in northwestern Crete, which is a region and not a point for the town; no archaeological site is identified and no readable page prints a point for the town itself (Pleiades is behind a bot challenge, ToposText gives the headland). The stored point lies in central-east Crete, far from that peninsula, and I found nothing to keep or replace it with.

The only sources for the town are the mention by Ptolemy and a passage in Juvenal (English Wikipedia, citing Smith's Dictionary), and Buondelmonti seeing remains in 1415; they say nothing about when the town began, and the town has no excavated site. The stored -800 is a rule value from Wikidata's Classical Antiquity; no source dates the start.

The site is a nature reserve declared in 1994 that contains several separate ruins; English Wikipedia dates Horvat Midras (about 2.5 km from the stored point) to the 10th century BCE onward, Horvat Lavnin from the Late Bronze and Iron Ages, Horvat Borgyn to the 2nd century CE, so the sources give different starts for different ruins inside it and none for the reserve as one site. The rule-made -3000 has no source.

English Wikipedia (Kunturmarka, Pasco: Paucartambo District, Pasco Province; round buildings and chullpa tombs) and Wikidata print no point; the MINCETUR inventory ficha it cites (cod_Ficha=876) shows no readable record text and no coordinates, and searches for Condormarca/Cunturmarka in Paucartambo District, Pasco found no study or register that prints a latitude and longitude. Namesakes (Kunturmarka in Ayacucho, Condormarca District in La Libertad, Ninamarca in Cusco) were not used.

English Wikipedia (Paphos Archaeological Park) names the Early Roman House only as one of the structures the Polish mission took up; it, the University of Warsaw news page and the Wikimedia Commons categories print no point for the building (Commons has coordinates only for the whole park, and Wikidata has no item). The PCMA season report page answers with a captcha. No readable page prints a point for this house.

No readable page dates the Early Roman House: English Wikipedia and the University of Warsaw news item only list it among the houses excavated by the Polish mission at Nea Paphos, with no construction date; the PCMA season report that might date it answers with a captcha, and the name alone is not a dated source. The rule-made start 43 therefore has no source.

The English Wikipedia article only calls the petroglyphs 'pre-historic' (a word the period vocabulary does not read from that spelling) and the Arabic article adds, without a citation, that the rock art is about nine thousand years old; both belong to one Wikipedia source family, give no checkable year, century or millennium, and no independent readable page (Saudipedia, Madain Project, the Hail/Jubbah pages and PDFs, which concern other sites or cannot be read by plain GET) dates Jabal al-Hayn.

No source dates the start of Siponto. English, German and Italian Wikipedia give only a Daunian foundation (legend of Diomedes) with no date, then events: Alexander of Epirus about 335 BC, a Roman colony of 189 or 194 BC. The Princeton Encyclopedia of Classical Sites calls it an ancient Daunian city occupied by Alexander of Molossos in 330 BC and a Roman colony in 194 BC; its 7th-6th c. BC limestone stelai are finds from the area, not a date for the town, and the city walls are said to be undated. Conquests and colony deductions are not the foundation, so the stored -500 is not confirmed and no replacement can be quoted.

Sources disagree about what counts as the start: the FAMSI report by Fitzsimmons (Chronology: Late Classic, core occupied c. AD 600-800) and Wikipedia date the royal centre to the Late Classic, but the same report and Wikipedia say the periphery was occupied considerably earlier, perhaps as far back as the late Preclassic. No readable page states a start year for the site as a whole that fits one bucket, so no quotable start is given; the stored AD 500 has no source.

The stored point is the centre of the dry Winnemucca Lake bed (enwiki 40°06'40"N 119°20'28"W), not the petroglyph site 26Wa3329 (WDL12), which lies at the western edge of the subbasin inside the Pyramid Lake Indian Reservation. The Megalithic Portal states its point is 'for the dry lakebed itself, and not the petroglyph site' and gives only a rounded 40.14, 119.3W; the USGS page and the Benson et al. paper pages (ScienceDirect, ResearchGate, Academia) show no readable point for the carvings, which are not publicly located. No quotable source prints the site's own point.

English Wikipedia: archaeologists have argued the stone was part of a destroyed fourth-millennium BCE long barrow, but the 2008-09 excavation found no evidence of a chambered long barrow and showed the megalith was placed in its present position only in the post-medieval period (1450 to 1600). The excavation could not date the prehistoric activity nearby. No source dates the site's start, so the Neolithic start from the Wikidata item stays unsupported.

Serpent's Wall is a system of earthworks of about 1,000 remaining km across the middle Dnieper; the English, Ukrainian, Russian and German Wikipedia articles and the Wikidata item print no point for it. Only single sections have points (the Ukrainian article on the southern section of the Kyiv-region walls near Kruhlyk and Khodosivka gives about 50.276, 30.467, about 3 km from the stored point, and the nature monument near Makariv about 50.46, 29.70), and a point of one section is not the point of the system, so no source can be quoted for the site's point.

No source gives a start for Saticula. English Wikipedia names it a Caudini city attacked by Rome in 343 BC, which is an event, not a foundation; its ceramic trade-network remark is undated, and the fossil section concerns an Early/Middle Pleistocene site of the same name in the Wikipedia article, not the town. Web searches on Sant'Agata de' Goti found the necropolis finds (excavated in the 18th century) with no date for the burials and a 313 BC date that belongs to the Roman colony. The stored -500 is a band edge with no source.

The Kültür Envanteri record and Lycian Monuments describe the rock tomb as carved into an isolated bedrock outcrop in the plain slightly north of the city's necropolis, but print no coordinates; the only printed points (Wikipedia 36°12′55″N 29°51′23″E, ToposText 36.2154, 29.8564) are for the city of Tyberissos, a different place, and the Commons photo geotags are camera positions, not a site point. No source quotes a point for the tomb itself.

The only dating of this Usnu (Umari district, Pachitea province, Huanuco; 2,833 m, Panaococha) is the tourism inventory text, reproduced at turismoperuano.com, that it 'floreció durante la época de los Chupachos', a local ethnic group named without a year or a period of the vocabulary; English and Spanish Wikipedia give no date, and no excavation report was found. A named culture with no dates is not a start year, and the stored 1 AD is a rule-made band edge with no source.

The article calls the earthwork enclosure 'The Battery' on St. John's Hill 'of undetermined age' and gives only a 1st-century AD Roman fort below the hill; the Megalithic Portal and Historic England pages could not be read by plain GET (403), and no readable page dates the earthwork. The Roman fort's date is not the start of this earthwork record, so no source dates it.

The entry 'Bema' is the generic term for an orator's platform (English Wikipedia's Bema article is about the term in Greek and Jewish use and prints no coordinates); no source identifies which bema the stored Athens point marks. ToposText places the Pnyx, whose bema it mentions, at 37.9715, 23.7193, a hill site about 0.6 km from the stored point and a different site, with no coordinates given for a bema itself.

Bema is a generic architectural term, not one datable monument; English Wikipedia gives no date for any bema and the Pnyx bema (ToposText: Classical to Hellenistic Pnyx, boundary stone about 450 BCE) is another site. No source dates the start of a site named Bema, so the stored -1500 stays unsourced.

No source dates the start of Banoštor (Bononia Malata). English Wikipedia's 279 BC is the Gallic invasion of the Balkans, with the Banoštor settlement inferred from it. The Princeton Encyclopedia of Classical Sites (Perseus) and EBSCO say only that, judging by the name Malata, it began as a Celtic or partly Celtic settlement, with no date, and Princeton dates the excavated house remains to the 1st-4th c. AD. Celtic is not a period word this lane reads, and the Roman-era remains do not show when the site began. So the stored -279 has no sound source.

The English Wikipedia article on Ruthergate (a disused old road near Guisborough) prints no coordinates and Wikidata Q7383368 holds none; the only nearby coordinates found belong to Ruther Cross, a different monument at the road's start, which lies more than 1 km from the stored point and is not the road's own point. No page prints a point for Ruthergate itself.

The only source that dates Llamachayuq/Llamachayoq (San Jeronimo, Andahuaylas) is the MINCETUR inventory ficha 8212, which says the petroglyph shelters belong to the 'periodo Arcaico - formativo'. That is a period of the Andean sequence that is not in this lane's period vocabulary (no 'archaic' or 'formative' entry), and the ficha gives no year; mapping it to a generic 'prehistoric' would only restate the rule-made start. The IFEA study (Los chancas, appendix 2) says petroglyphs are hard to date, that most in the sierra are presumed preceramic or early ceramic (a class statement, not this site) and notes a Christian cross at Llamachayoc, i.e. at least some post-contact carvings. No source gives a start year or a vocabulary period for the site.

No readable page prints a point for the Hoyo Negro pit itself. English Wikipedia has no Hoyo Negro article; its Naia article only places Hoyo Negro in the Sistema Sac Actun, and the one printed point nearby (20.2466, -87.4641) is the Wikipedia point of the whole Sac Actun cave system, not of this pit. The stored point is that system point. The stored source page chei.ucsd.edu answered 403 to a plain request (a throttle, not a finding) and I found no other page with a point.
